# SURVEY_EXP audit checklist (v0.15, generated by scripts/skillgen)

24 checks. Each rests on claims from the methods literature, and each one points to where to read more. The 23 sources listed under **Sources** below are the ones cited in the further-reading lines.

**How to read a verdict.** `PASS` / `FLAG` are decided by the stated conditions. `NA` means the check is out of scope for this design - never that the paper was silent. When a check applies and the paper says nothing, the verdict is the one given in *When silent*.

**Evidence scope.** A verdict covers only the text the audit could see. A FLAG on material the paper says is in an appendix or replication package means "not shown here", not "not done" - such flags carry that caveat in the report.

**Thresholds are rules of thumb unless marked otherwise.** Where a cutoff is conventional rather than derived, the item says so, and near-threshold values are reported as borderline rather than silently rounded to a verdict.

## Scope triggers

A check applies only when its scope trigger fires. Triggers key on the paper's own explicit stance and default OUT when the paper is silent.

- **`all`** - Every survey experiment in the corpus.
- **`list_experiment`** - The paper states it uses a list experiment / item-count technique - respondents in a treatment group receive a list containing a sensitive item and report only a count. Fires on the paper's own naming of a list/item-count/unmatched-count design. Does NOT fire on a direct sensitive question, a randomized-response design, or an endorsement design.
- **`nonrandomized_moderator`** - The paper states it estimates or interprets the effect of a variable it did NOT randomly assign - a measured respondent characteristic, attitude, exposure, or covariate used as an explanatory, moderating, or mediating variable in a causal claim. Fires when the paper reads a non-randomized variable's association as its effect. Does NOT fire on effects of the randomized treatment itself, nor on associations the paper explicitly labels non-causal.
- **`conjoint`** - The paper states it uses a conjoint / fully-randomized attribute design in which respondents evaluate profiles whose attributes are independently randomized. Fires on the paper's own naming of a conjoint or randomized-attribute profile design. Does NOT fire on a single-vignette design that manipulates one or two features, nor on a list/endorsement design.
- **`factor_isolation_claim`** - The paper states its manipulation isolates the effect of one specific factor, attributing the treatment-control difference to that single factor. A design presented only as estimating the combined effect of a bundled treatment, with no claim to isolate one factor, does NOT fire it.
- **`endorsement_experiment`** - The paper states it uses an endorsement experiment - respondents rate policies, and a randomly assigned subset sees the policy endorsed by an actor. Fires on the paper's own naming of an endorsement design. Does NOT fire on a list experiment or a direct actor-approval question.
- **`belief_effect`** - The paper states its estimand is the effect of a belief or of respondents' understanding of a manipulated attribute (an epistemic effect) - it interprets its manipulation as changing what respondents believe about a focal factor. Fires on the paper's own framing of the quantity of interest as a belief/attribute effect. Does NOT fire on a design that interprets its manipulation only as the effect of the message/wording itself, with no belief-level claim.
- **`mediation`** - The paper states it performs a mediation analysis or decomposes an effect through a mediator that it measured rather than randomized. Fires on the paper's own naming of a mediator / indirect effect with an observed mediator. Does NOT fire on a design that randomizes the mediator in a factorial arm, nor on a paper with no mediation claim.
- **`subgroup_or_conditioning`** - The paper states it estimates a subgroup, conditional, or moderated effect, or conditions/subsets its estimate on a respondent-measured variable. Fires when the paper reports heterogeneous effects by a respondent variable, interacts treatment with a covariate, or conditions on a post-treatment quantity. Does NOT fire on a paper reporting only a single overall treatment effect with no conditioning.
- **`direct_list_comparison`** - The paper states it reads the gap between a direct-question estimate and a list-experiment (or other indirect) estimate as a measure of sensitivity or social-desirability bias. A list experiment alone, a direct question alone, or using both only to triangulate a prevalence without interpreting their difference as bias, does NOT fire it.
- **`survey_weights`** - The paper states it applies survey/selection/sampling weights in estimating a population-level (PATE) effect. Reporting demographics or design features without using weights in estimation does NOT fire it.
- **`list_regression`** - The paper states it estimates a regression model (linear least squares, nonlinear least squares, or maximum likelihood) relating respondent covariates to list-experiment responses. Fires when the paper names such a multivariate list-experiment estimator. Does NOT fire on a paper reporting only a difference-in-means prevalence or unadjusted subgroup means.
- **`list_predictor`** - The paper states it uses a list-experiment quantity (a predicted/fitted sensitive-item value or estimated proportion) as an explanatory variable in a further outcome model - a two-step or multi-stage procedure. Fires on the paper's own description of feeding a list-experiment estimate into a downstream regression. Does NOT fire on a one-stage list-experiment analysis that reports prevalence or covariate associations directly.
- **`repeated_tasks`** - The paper states each respondent contributes more than one observation to the analysis - multiple conjoint tasks, repeated rating/choice tasks, repeated vignettes, or multiple items analyzed jointly per respondent. Fires on the paper's own description of a within-respondent repeated-measures structure. Does NOT fire on a between-subjects design where each respondent contributes a single observation.
- **`population_inference`** - The paper states it generalizes its treatment-effect estimate to a real-world or target population - it describes its estimand as a population effect, claims representativeness, or applies survey weights to a population. Fires on the paper's own generalization/representativeness language. Does NOT fire on a paper that explicitly confines its claims to the study sample or presents itself as an internal-validity demonstration.
- **`framing_treatment`** - The paper states it compares two or more substantive framing/wording/message arms to estimate a treatment effect on attitudes. Fires when the design contrasts message or frame conditions. Does NOT fire on list/conjoint/endorsement measurement designs where a control list or reference category is intrinsic to the method.

## IDENT

*Identification - the assumptions the causal claim rests on.*

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-01 - A survey experiment must state that assignment to its conditions was random.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should state that respondents were assigned to experimental conditions (such as arms, lists, or profiles) at random.

**Why it matters:** Random assignment makes the groups alike on average, so a difference in outcomes can be read as the effect of the treatment.

**Check:** Whether the paper states that respondents were assigned to conditions (arms, lists, profiles) at random.

- **Pass:** The paper states that assignment to experimental conditions was randomized.
- **Flag:** The paper reports an experimental contrast but never states that assignment was random.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Eva Anduiza, Aina Gallego, & Jordi Muñoz. (2013). Turning a Blind Eye. Comparative Political Studies, 46(12), 1664-1692. https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414013489081 - p. 1671
  - Kosuke Imai. (2011). Multivariate Regression Analysis for the Item Count Technique. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106(494), 407-416. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2011.ap10415 - p. 409
  - James G. Kane, Stephen C. Craig, & Kenneth D. Wald. (2004). Religion and Presidential Politics in Florida: A List Experiment<sup>*</sup>. Social Science Quarterly, 85(2), 281-293. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0038-4941.2004.08502004.x - p. 284

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-02 - A list-experiment paper must state or address the no-design-effect identifying assumption.

**Scope:** `list_experiment` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (8 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper using a list experiment (where respondents report how many items on a list apply to them) should state or address the assumption that adding the sensitive item does not change answers to the other items.

**Why it matters:** The estimate of how common the sensitive item is holds only if adding it leaves each respondent's count of the other items unchanged; otherwise the estimate is mismeasured.

**Check:** Whether the paper states, or otherwise addresses, the assumption that the sensitive item does not shift control-item answers.

- **Pass:** The paper states the no-design-effect assumption (that appending the sensitive item leaves control-item responses unchanged) or otherwise addresses it.
- **Flag:** The paper analyzes a list experiment without ever stating or addressing the no-design-effect assumption.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - p. 51
  - Belén González & Richard Traunmüller. (2023). The political consequences of wartime sexual violence: Evidence from a list experiment. Journal of Peace Research, 61(6), 1035-1050. https://doi.org/10.1177/00223433231183992 - p. 1041
  - Kosuke Imai. (2011). Multivariate Regression Analysis for the Item Count Technique. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106(494), 407-416. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2011.ap10415 - p. 409

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-03 - List-experiment identification also requires that treated respondents report the sensitive item truthfully within their count (the no-liars condition); the paper must acknowledge this condition and speak to its plausibility.

**Scope:** `list_experiment` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (10 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A list-experiment paper should acknowledge that respondents shown the sensitive item must count it truthfully, and should discuss whether truthful reporting is plausible for its item.

**Why it matters:** The list-experiment estimate is valid only if respondents report the sensitive item honestly within their count.

**Check:** Whether the paper states the no-liars / truthful-response condition for the sensitive item.

- **Pass:** The paper names the no-liars condition and addresses whether truthful reporting is plausible for its item.
- **Flag:** The paper analyzes a list experiment without acknowledging that its validity depends on truthful reporting of the sensitive item.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - p. 52
  - Graeme Blair, Winston Chou, & Kosuke Imai. (2019). List Experiments with Measurement Error. Political Analysis, 27(4), 455-480. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.56 - p. 458
  - Adam Glynn. (2013). What Can We Learn with Statistical Truth Serum?. Public Opinion Quarterly, 77(S1), 159-172. https://doi.org/10.1093/poq/nfs070 - p. 162
  - Kosuke Imai. (2011). Multivariate Regression Analysis for the Item Count Technique. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106(494), 407-416. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2011.ap10415 - p. 409

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-04 - A causal claim about a non-randomized covariate or moderator must state the exogeneity / no-unobserved-confounding assumption it rests on.

**Scope:** `nonrandomized_moderator` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper reads the effect of a variable that was not randomly assigned as causal, it should state the assumption that no unmeasured factor drives both that variable and the outcome, or label the relationship as not causal.

**Why it matters:** Random assignment supports causal claims only about the randomized treatment, so causal claims about other variables rest on this further assumption.

**Check:** Whether, when the paper interprets a non-randomized variable's effect causally, it states the identifying assumption (no unobserved confounding / exogeneity) that would license that reading.

- **Pass:** The paper states the identifying assumption (exogeneity / no unobserved confounding) that would license the causal reading of the non-randomized variable, or explicitly labels the relationship as non-causal.
- **Flag:** The paper interprets a non-randomized variable's effect causally without stating any exogeneity / no-confounding assumption.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - p. 50
  - Belén González & Richard Traunmüller. (2023). The political consequences of wartime sexual violence: Evidence from a list experiment. Journal of Peace Research, 61(6), 1035-1050. https://doi.org/10.1177/00223433231183992 - p. 1044
  - Julia C. Morse & Tyler Pratt. (2022). Strategies of Contestation: International Law, Domestic Audiences, and Image Management. The Journal of Politics, 84(4), 2080-2093. https://doi.org/10.1086/719418 - p. 2090

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-05 - A multi-task conjoint paper must state or address the stability / no-carryover assumption.

**Scope:** `conjoint` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A conjoint paper (where respondents choose among profiles with randomly varied attributes) that gives each respondent several tasks should state or address the assumption that answers in one task are unaffected by profiles seen in other tasks.

**Why it matters:** Estimating attribute effects from several tasks per respondent requires that responses stay stable across tasks and do not carry over from other tasks.

**Check:** Whether the paper states or addresses the stability / no-carryover assumption across a respondent's tasks.

- **Pass:** The paper states or addresses the stability / no-carryover assumption (potential outcomes stable across tasks, unaffected by other tasks' profiles).
- **Flag:** The paper analyzes a multi-task conjoint without stating or addressing stability / no-carryover across tasks.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Jens Hainmueller, Daniel J. Hopkins, & Teppei Yamamoto. (2013). Causal Inference in Conjoint Analysis: Understanding Multidimensional Choices via Stated Preference Experiments. Political Analysis, 22(1), 1-30. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt024 - p. 8

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-06 - A conjoint paper must confine its causal quantities to attribute combinations the randomization assigns positive probability, or acknowledge the restriction.

**Scope:** `conjoint` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A conjoint paper should limit its causal claims to attribute combinations that the randomization could actually produce, or acknowledge where some combinations were excluded.

**Why it matters:** Effects can be estimated only for combinations that had a chance of being shown; going beyond them requires extra assumptions.

**Check:** Whether the paper's randomization assigns positive probability to every attribute combination whose effect it analyzes (or the paper acknowledges the restricted support where combinations are excluded).

- **Pass:** The paper's attributes are randomized so that every analyzed attribute combination has positive assignment probability, or the paper restricts its causal claims to the combinations actually assigned.
- **Flag:** The paper analyzes conjoint effects over attribute combinations that its randomization excludes or never assigns, without acknowledging the restricted support.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Jens Hainmueller, Daniel J. Hopkins, & Teppei Yamamoto. (2013). Causal Inference in Conjoint Analysis: Understanding Multidimensional Choices via Stated Preference Experiments. Political Analysis, 22(1), 1-30. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt024 - pp. 9, 20

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-07 - A contrast can be attributed to one intended factor only if the compared conditions differ solely on that factor (or the effect operates only through the intended channel); a paper that claims to isolate one factor must either state/defend that single-factor (single-channel) isolation or acknowledge that the contrast bundles several differences and limit its attribution accordingly.

**Scope:** `factor_isolation_claim` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (7 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper credits an effect to one factor, it should defend that the compared conditions differ only on that factor (or that the effect works only through the intended channel), or acknowledge that the conditions differ in several ways and limit its claims.

**Why it matters:** If the conditions differ in more than one way, the effect cannot be credited to the single intended factor.

**Check:** Whether the paper, when it attributes an effect to one intended factor, either states/defends that its conditions differ only on that factor (or that the effect operates only through the intended channel) or acknowledges that the contrast bundles multiple differences.

- **Pass:** The paper states or defends that its compared conditions differ only on the named factor (or that the effect operates only through the intended causal channel), or acknowledges that the contrast bundles multiple differences and limits its attribution accordingly.
- **Flag:** The paper attributes the effect to one intended factor without either defending single-factor/single-channel isolation or acknowledging that its conditions differ on additional dimensions it does not account for.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Stephen Chaudoin. (2014). Promises or Policies? An Experimental Analysis of International Agreements and Audience Reactions. International Organization, 68(1), 235-256. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0020818313000386 - pp. 239-240
  - Allan Dafoe, Baobao Zhang, & Devin Caughey. (2018). Information Equivalence in Survey Experiments. Political Analysis, 26(4), 399-416. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.9 - p. 414
  - Daryl G. Press, Scott D. Sagan, & Benjamin Valentino. (2013). Atomic Aversion: Experimental Evidence on Taboos, Traditions, and the Non-Use of Nuclear Weapons. American Political Science Review, 107(1), 188-206. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055412000597 - p. 201

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-08 - An endorsement-experiment paper must state or address the no-interpretation-change identifying assumption.

**Scope:** `endorsement_experiment` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper using an endorsement experiment (where a policy is shown with or without a group's endorsement) should state or address the assumption that the endorsement does not change how respondents understand the policy.

**Why it matters:** If the endorsement changes how respondents understand the policy, the measured shift reflects that changed understanding rather than support for the endorser.

**Check:** Whether the paper states or addresses the assumption that the endorsement does not change respondents' interpretation of the policy.

- **Pass:** The paper states or addresses the no-interpretation-change identifying assumption (endorsement shifts support, not policy understanding).
- **Flag:** The paper interprets endorsement effects as support without stating or addressing the no-interpretation-change assumption.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Will Bullock, Kosuke Imai, & Jacob N. Shapiro. (2011). Statistical Analysis of Endorsement Experiments: Measuring Support for Militant Groups in Pakistan. Political Analysis, 19(4), 363-384. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr031 - p. 370

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-09 - An endorsement paper pooling multiple policy items must state or test the single-dimension assumption.

**Scope:** `endorsement_experiment` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** An endorsement-experiment paper that combines several policy items into one measure should state, or test, the assumption that the items share a single underlying dimension.

**Why it matters:** Combining the items presumes they belong to one policy domain, and standard difference-in-means and regression cannot properly combine them.

**Check:** Whether the paper that pools multiple endorsement policy items states (or tests) the assumption that they share a single dimension/domain.

- **Pass:** The paper states the single-dimension / shared-domain assumption behind pooling its endorsement items, or reports a test of it.
- **Flag:** The paper pools multiple endorsement policy items into one measure without stating or testing that they share a single dimension.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair, Kosuke Imai, & Jason Lyall. (2014). Comparing and Combining List and Endorsement Experiments: Evidence from Afghanistan. American Journal of Political Science, 58(4), 1043-1063. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12086 - p. 1047
  - Jason Lyall, Graeme Blair, & Kosuke Imai. (2013). Explaining Support for Combatants during Wartime: A Survey Experiment in Afghanistan. American Political Science Review, 107(4), 679-705. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055413000403 - p. 682

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-10 - A paper claiming a belief/epistemic effect must state the information-equivalence assumption.

**Scope:** `belief_effect` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper that reads its manipulation as an effect of respondents' beliefs should state the information-equivalence assumption: that the conditions are equivalent on background features.

**Why it matters:** Random assignment alone does not support a claim that the effect works through beliefs about the focal factor; that claim also requires the conditions to be equivalent on background features.

**Check:** Whether the paper states the information-equivalence assumption when it interprets its manipulation as a belief/epistemic effect.

- **Pass:** The paper states the information-equivalence assumption (conditions equivalent on background features) as a condition for its belief-effect interpretation.
- **Flag:** The paper interprets its manipulation as the effect of a belief without stating the information-equivalence assumption.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Allan Dafoe, Baobao Zhang, & Devin Caughey. (2018). Information Equivalence in Survey Experiments. Political Analysis, 26(4), 399-416. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.9 - pp. 399-400

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-11 - A mediation analysis with an observed mediator must state its sequential-ignorability assumption.

**Scope:** `mediation` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper that studies how an effect passes through a measured, not randomized, intermediate variable (a mediator) should state the sequential-ignorability assumption: that nothing beyond the treatment and pretreatment covariates confounds the link between the mediator and the outcome.

**Why it matters:** Because the mediator was not randomized, this analysis reintroduces the risk of omitted-variable bias.

**Check:** Whether the paper states the sequential-ignorability / no-unmeasured-mediator-outcome-confounding assumption for its observed mediator.

- **Pass:** The paper states the sequential-ignorability / no-unmeasured-confounding assumption required for its observed-mediator analysis.
- **Flag:** The paper performs mediation with an observed mediator without stating the sequential-ignorability / no-confounding assumption.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Avidit Acharya, Matthew Blackwell, & Maya Sen. (2018). Analyzing Causal Mechanisms in Survey Experiments. Political Analysis, 26(4), 357-378. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.19 - pp. 361, 363

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-12 - Subgroup/conditioning variables must be pretreatment, or shown unaffected by treatment.

**Scope:** `subgroup_or_conditioning` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** Variables used to split the sample or define subgroups should be measured before treatment, or the paper should show the treatment did not affect them.

**Why it matters:** Conditioning on a variable measured after treatment can bias results and change what is being estimated.

**Check:** Whether the variable the paper conditions/subsets on is pretreatment, or, if measured post-treatment, whether the paper shows treatment did not affect it.

- **Pass:** The conditioning/moderating variable is measured pretreatment, or the paper demonstrates that treatment did not affect a post-treatment conditioning variable.
- **Flag:** The paper conditions on or subsets by a variable measured after treatment without showing the treatment left it uncontaminated.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Avidit Acharya, Matthew Blackwell, & Maya Sen. (2018). Analyzing Causal Mechanisms in Survey Experiments. Political Analysis, 26(4), 357-378. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.19 - p. 370
  - Stephen Chaudoin. (2014). Promises or Policies? An Experimental Analysis of International Agreements and Audience Reactions. International Organization, 68(1), 235-256. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0020818313000386 - p. 246
  - Jonathan Mummolo & Erik Peterson. (2018). Demand Effects in Survey Experiments: An Empirical Assessment. American Political Science Review, 113(2), 517-529. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055418000837 - p. 527

### SURVEY_EXP-IDENT-13 - The gap between a list-experiment estimate and a direct-question estimate can be read as sensitivity/social-desirability bias only if the list assumptions hold and, further, there is no differential nonresponse, no order or wording effects, and a common population; a paper making this interpretation must state those auxiliary assumptions.

**Scope:** `direct_list_comparison` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper reading the gap between list-experiment and direct-question estimates as sensitivity bias should state the assumptions this needs (the list assumptions, no differences in nonresponse, no order or wording effects, and a common population), or note that without them the gap may reflect only the measurement methods.

**Why it matters:** Without these assumptions, the gap may reflect only the difference between the two measurement methods.

**Check:** Whether the paper interpreting the list-minus-direct gap as sensitivity bias states the required auxiliary assumptions (list assumptions plus no differential nonresponse/order/wording, common population).

- **Pass:** The paper states the auxiliary assumptions its bias interpretation needs, or notes that without them the gap only reflects the measurement technology.
- **Flag:** The paper reads the list-versus-direct difference as sensitivity bias without stating the auxiliary assumptions it requires.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair, Alexander Coppock, & Margaret Moor. (2020). When to Worry about Sensitivity Bias: A Social Reference Theory and Evidence from 30 Years of List Experiments. American Political Science Review, 114(4), 1297-1315. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055420000374 - pp. 1307, 1311
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - p. 62

## EST

*Estimation - whether the estimator recovers the target parameter.*

### SURVEY_EXP-EST-01 - A list-experiment paper should not present multivariate covariate models of the sensitive trait, without caveat, when the estimated prevalence is negative or indistinguishable from zero.

**Scope:** `list_experiment` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A list-experiment paper should not model how the sensitive trait relates to several respondent characteristics, without a caveat, when the estimated share holding the trait is negative or not distinguishable from zero.

**Why it matters:** A trait must actually be present to vary with respondent characteristics, so such models are unreliable when almost no one holds it.

**Check:** Whether the paper presents a multivariate covariate model of the sensitive trait while its estimated prevalence is negative or not distinguishable from zero.

- **Pass:** Either the paper presents no multivariate covariate model of the sensitive trait, or where it does the estimated prevalence is clearly positive (point estimate positive and not statistically indistinguishable from zero).
- **Flag:** The paper presents a multivariate covariate model of the sensitive trait while its estimated prevalence is negative or statistically indistinguishable from zero, with no stated caveat about the trait's rarity limiting model reliability.
- **When silent:** PASS
- **Threshold:** cutoff 0.0; provenance: rule of thumb; borderline band: [0.0, 0.05]
- **Inside the band:** Below the cutoff (estimated prevalence negative): FLAG if a multivariate covariate model is presented without a caveat about unreliability. In the border band (prevalence non-negative but statistically indistinguishable from zero, i.e. its confidence interval includes zero): FLAG if a multivariate model is presented without a stated caveat about the trait's rarity limiting model reliability. Above the band (prevalence point estimate positive and its interval excludes zero): PASS.

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair, Winston Chou, & Kosuke Imai. (2019). List Experiments with Measurement Error. Political Analysis, 27(4), 455-480. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.56 - pp. 457, 468
  - Graeme Blair, Winston Chou, & Kosuke Imai. (2010). list: Statistical Methods for the Item Count Technique and List Experiment. CRAN: Contributed Packages. https://doi.org/10.32614/cran.package.list - p. 457

### SURVEY_EXP-EST-02 - A survey-weighted population (PATE) estimator is derived assuming the weights are correct and known and that treatment assignment is independent of selection, and it can be arbitrarily biased when an unmodeled selection mechanism makes the weights wrong; a paper using weights to estimate a population effect must state these assumptions or acknowledge weight-misspecification bias.

**Scope:** `survey_weights` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper using survey weights to estimate a population-wide effect should state that this assumes correct, known weights and treatment assignment independent of selection into the sample, or acknowledge bias from wrong weights.

**Why it matters:** If an unmodeled selection process makes the weights wrong, the weighted estimate can be badly biased.

**Check:** Whether the paper using survey weights for a population effect states the assumptions its weighted estimator relies on (correct/known weights, assignment independent of selection) or acknowledges weight-misspecification bias.

- **Pass:** The paper states the selection/weighting assumptions behind its weighted PATE estimate, or acknowledges the bias possible when the weights are misspecified.
- **Flag:** The paper reports a survey-weighted population effect without stating the weighting/selection assumptions or acknowledging weight-misspecification bias.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Luke Miratrix, Jasjeet S. Sekhon, Alexander G. Theodoridis, & Luis Fernando Reglero Campos. (2018). Worth Weighting? How to Think About and Use Weights in Survey Experiments. Political Analysis, 26(3), 275-291. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.1 - pp. 283, 287-289

## INFER

*Inference - standard errors, tests, and their validity.*

### SURVEY_EXP-INFER-01 - A linear-regression list-experiment analysis must use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.

**Scope:** `list_regression` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A list-experiment paper using linear regression should report heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, which allow the spread of errors to differ across groups.

**Why it matters:** The error spread differs by treatment status in this regression, so ordinary standard errors are wrong.

**Check:** Whether the reported standard errors for the list-experiment regression are heteroskedasticity-robust.

- **Pass:** The paper reports heteroskedasticity-robust (heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors for its linear list-experiment regression.
- **Flag:** The paper reports a linear list-experiment regression with ordinary (non-robust) standard errors.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - p. 53
  - Kosuke Imai. (2011). Multivariate Regression Analysis for the Item Count Technique. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106(494), 407-416. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2011.ap10415 - p. 409

### SURVEY_EXP-INFER-02 - A two-step list-experiment-as-predictor analysis must propagate first-stage uncertainty into its standard errors.

**Scope:** `list_predictor` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper uses a list-experiment estimate as an input to a second model, its standard errors should include the uncertainty from the first estimate.

**Why it matters:** Plugging in first-stage estimates as if they were known gets neither the coefficient nor the standard error right.

**Check:** Whether the paper's standard errors for the downstream model incorporate first-stage (list-experiment) estimation uncertainty, via bootstrap or an analytic multi-stage variance.

- **Pass:** The paper's two-stage standard errors incorporate the uncertainty from both the list-experiment stage and the outcome stage.
- **Flag:** The paper feeds a list-experiment estimate into an outcome model but reports standard errors that ignore the first-stage uncertainty.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Kosuke Imai, Bethany Park, & Kenneth F. Greene. (2014). Using the Predicted Responses from List Experiments as Explanatory Variables in Regression Models. Political Analysis, 23(2), 180-196. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu017 - pp. 182, 187
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - p. 57

### SURVEY_EXP-INFER-03 - A repeated-within-respondent design must account for within-respondent dependence in its standard errors.

**Scope:** `repeated_tasks` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When each respondent gives several answers, the standard errors should account for this, by clustering on respondent or using a respondent-level bootstrap.

**Why it matters:** Answers from the same respondent are related, so default standard errors that treat them as independent are not valid.

**Check:** Whether the paper's standard errors account for within-respondent dependence (respondent-clustered SEs or a respondent-level block bootstrap).

- **Pass:** The paper reports respondent-clustered standard errors or a respondent-level block bootstrap for its repeated-measures analysis.
- **Flag:** The paper analyzes repeated within-respondent observations with default standard errors that ignore the within-respondent correlation.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Jens Hainmueller, Daniel J. Hopkins, & Teppei Yamamoto. (2013). Causal Inference in Conjoint Analysis: Understanding Multidimensional Choices via Stated Preference Experiments. Political Analysis, 22(1), 1-30. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt024 - pp. 16-17
  - Avidit Acharya, Matthew Blackwell, & Maya Sen. (2018). Analyzing Causal Mechanisms in Survey Experiments. Political Analysis, 26(4), 357-378. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.19 - p. 371

## ROBUST

*Robustness - sensitivity, diagnostics, and alternative specifications.*

### SURVEY_EXP-ROBUST-01 - A list-experiment paper should report a diagnostic (respondent-type proportions or a design-effect test) bearing on its identifying assumptions.

**Scope:** `list_experiment` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (7 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A list-experiment paper should report a check on its key assumptions, such as estimated shares of respondent types or a formal test for design effects (the sensitive item changing answers to other items).

**Why it matters:** A negative estimated share of a respondent type signals that an assumption fails, and a formal test can detect a violation.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports a diagnostic for identification-assumption violations - estimated respondent-type proportions and/or a formal design-effect test.

- **Pass:** The paper reports estimated respondent-type proportions and/or a formal design-effect (assumption-violation) test as a diagnostic on its list-experiment identifying assumptions.
- **Flag:** The paper reports a list-experiment estimate but no proportion-based or test-based diagnostic for the identifying assumptions.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - pp. 64, 72

### SURVEY_EXP-ROBUST-02 - A belief-effect paper should report placebo/balance tests on background beliefs to probe information equivalence.

**Scope:** `belief_effect` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper claiming an effect through beliefs should report placebo or balance tests showing whether background beliefs or attributes are similar across conditions.

**Why it matters:** These tests check information equivalence; if background features differ, the result can no longer be read as a belief effect.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports a placebo / balance test on background beliefs or attributes to probe information equivalence.

- **Pass:** The paper reports a placebo or balance test on background beliefs/attributes bearing on information equivalence.
- **Flag:** The paper claims a belief effect but reports no placebo/balance test on background beliefs.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Allan Dafoe, Baobao Zhang, & Devin Caughey. (2018). Information Equivalence in Survey Experiments. Political Analysis, 26(4), 399-416. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.9 - pp. 401, 404

## REPORT

*Reporting - what the paper must state for a reader to evaluate it.*

### SURVEY_EXP-REPORT-01 - A conjoint paper reporting AMCEs must state the attribute distribution used to average them.

**Scope:** `conjoint` · **Severity if flagged:** LOW · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A conjoint paper reporting AMCEs (average marginal component effects, the average effect of one attribute level) should state and justify the distribution of the other attributes used to average them.

**Why it matters:** An AMCE depends on that distribution, and any target distribution should lie within the combinations the experiment actually used.

**Check:** Whether the paper states the distribution of the other attributes used to average its reported AMCEs.

- **Pass:** The paper states (and justifies) the distribution over the remaining attributes used to compute its AMCEs.
- **Flag:** The paper reports AMCEs without stating the attribute distribution used to average them.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Jens Hainmueller, Daniel J. Hopkins, & Teppei Yamamoto. (2013). Causal Inference in Conjoint Analysis: Understanding Multidimensional Choices via Stated Preference Experiments. Political Analysis, 22(1), 1-30. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt024 - p. 12

### SURVEY_EXP-REPORT-02 - A paper generalizing to a population must state its sampling/weighting basis or an explicit generalization assumption.

**Scope:** `population_inference` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (7 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A paper that generalizes its result to a population should state the basis: a probability sample with proper weights, or an explicit assumption it argues for, such as representativeness or similar effects across people.

**Why it matters:** How a convenience sample relates to the population is generally unknown, and matching or reweighting on demographics does not settle it.

**Check:** Whether the paper that generalizes to a population states the basis for the generalization (probability sampling + weights, or an explicit assumption), rather than generalizing from a convenience/non-probability sample without justification.

- **Pass:** The paper states the basis for its population claim - a probability sample with appropriate weighting, or an explicit representativeness / effect-homogeneity assumption it argues for.
- **Flag:** The paper generalizes its estimate to a population from a convenience or non-probability sample without stating a supporting assumption or design basis.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Kevin Mullinix, Thomas J. Leeper, James Druckman, & Jeremy Freese. (2015). The Generalizability of Survey Experiments. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 2(2), 109-138. https://doi.org/10.1017/xps.2015.19 - pp. 114, 123-124

## DATA

*Data - sample construction and measurement.*

### SURVEY_EXP-DATA-01 - A list-experiment paper should address ceiling and floor effects in its design or analysis.

**Scope:** `list_experiment` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (7 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A list-experiment paper should address ceiling and floor effects (respondents who would say yes to all or none of the items), through its choice of items or a correction or diagnostic.

**Why it matters:** These effects bias the estimated share downward and remove the privacy the design relies on.

**Check:** Whether the paper addresses ceiling/floor effects, through control-item selection that avoids uniform response patterns or through a statistical correction or diagnostic.

- **Pass:** The paper addresses ceiling/floor effects - via control-item choice designed to avoid all-yes/all-no patterns, or via a correction or diagnostic for them.
- **Flag:** The paper analyzes a list experiment without addressing ceiling or floor effects in design or analysis.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Graeme Blair & Kosuke Imai. (2012). Statistical Analysis of List Experiments. Political Analysis, 20(1), 47-77. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr048 - pp. 66, 72
  - Kosuke Imai. (2011). Multivariate Regression Analysis for the Item Count Technique. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106(494), 407-416. https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2011.ap10415 - p. 408

### SURVEY_EXP-DATA-02 - A framing/wording experiment must include a control baseline or qualify conclusions when one is omitted.

**Scope:** `framing_treatment` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** A framing or wording experiment should include a no-treatment control group, or qualify its conclusions if it deliberately leaves one out.

**Why it matters:** Without a control, a difference between frames cannot show which frame moved attitudes.

**Check:** Whether the design includes a no-treatment control/baseline condition, or, if it is deliberately omitted, whether the paper qualifies its conclusions.

- **Pass:** The paper includes a no-treatment control/baseline arm, or, where one is deliberately omitted, qualifies its conclusions accordingly.
- **Flag:** The paper compares treatment/framing arms with no control baseline and does not qualify its conclusions.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Brian J. Gaines, James H. Kuklinski, & Paul J. Quirk. (2006). The Logic of the Survey Experiment Reexamined. Political Analysis, 15(1), 1-20. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpl008 - pp. 3, 9, 17
